summary: The article profiles Marcus Urann, the Maine-born lawyer turned cranberry farmer who made cranberries a Thanksgiving staple by inventing canned cranberry sauce in 1912 and co-founding Ocean Spray. It also covers his earlier role founding the society that became Phi Kappa Phi and notes there is no evidence the Pilgrims ate cranberries at the first Thanksgiving. Urann's innovations, including wet-harvesting, turned a short-season local fruit into a year-round international industry.
one_line: Marcus Urann, the 'Cranberry King,' invented canned cranberry sauce, co-founded Ocean Spray and founded the society that became Phi Kappa Phi.
key_facts: Marcus Libby Urann was born on Oct. 3, 1873, in Sullivan, Maine, to Marcus M. and Chestina Urann, and died on April 1, 1963 in Hanson, Massachusetts.

At the University of Maine, Urann founded a society of elite students, the Lambda Sigma Eta Society, renamed Phi Kappa Phi in 1900; it now has chapters at more than 325 U.S. campuses and as far away as the Philippines.
Urann gave up his Boston law practice in 1906 and bought his first cranberry bog on Cape Cod.
In 1912 Urann began processing gelled cranberries in cans, creating cranberry sauce and letting the fruit be sold year-round far from where it was grown.
Cranberries have only a brief harvest from late September to early November and a short shelf life, so before canning they were known fresh only in a few regions.
Urann pioneered wet-harvesting: because each berry holds four chambers of air and floats, a bog could be flooded and the berries agitated off the vines.
Urann teamed with John Makepeace and Elizabeth Lee to create Ocean Spray, still headquartered in Massachusetts; it first sold its cranberry sauce nationally in 1941.

Brian Wick of Massachusetts Cranberries says there is no evidence the Pilgrims had cranberries at the first Thanksgiving; Edward Winslow's account mentions only fowl, deer and 'our harvest being gotten in.'
Ocean Spray says fresh cranberries account for only 5% of the fruit's production today.
American farmers grow twice as many cranberries as No. 2 Canada and about 20 times third-place Chile, per the Cranberry Institute; Wisconsin surpassed Massachusetts decades ago as top state grower.
Ocean Spray reports six out of 10 Americans say cranberry sauce will always be on their Thanksgiving table, and over one third 'can't live without' it.
The Boston Globe's April 4 obituary called Urann a 'recognized giant of the cranberry industry' and the 'Cranberry King.'
Urann told the Associated Press in 1959: 'everything in life is what you do for others.'
